newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-TIGER EARNS HIS STRIPES WITH PLAYOFF VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TIGER EARNS HIS STRIPES WITH PLAYOFF VICTORY.

text.p: The future is now for 20-year-old Tiger Woods, who justified the great expectations of the golf world by pulling off a stunning playoff victory Sunday in his fifth tournament as a professional.

Forty-two days after winning an unprecedented third successive U.S. Amateur championship, Woods overcame a deficit of four with a final-round 64 and beat the formidable Davis Love III in sudden-death at Las Vegas for a $297,000 victory.
"He's going to be the next great player out here, obviously," said an admiring Love, a 10-time winner on the tour at age 32.
Jack Nicklaus, the modern-day giant of golf with an amazing 18 Grand Slam titles to his credit, had guaranteed greatness for Woods six months earlier at Augusta.
Nicklaus, a six-time winner of the Masters, and four-time champion Arnold Palmer played a practice round with Woods before this year's championship last April.

The Golden Bear marvelled at Woods's swing, his power and poise, and predicted the amateur had the talent to win more Masters than he and Palmer combined. "He'll be the favourite to win this thing for the next 20 years," gushed Nicklaus.
Nickluas may have been only slightly exaggerating.

In his first five, pressure-packed events as a pro chasing enough prize money to qualify as a regular on tour next year, Woods charted an extraordinary progression -- 50th to 11th to fifth to third to first. That adds up to $437,194 in earnings.
Though way early in the game, comparisons between Woods and the young Nicklaus, who twice won the U.S. Amateur, seem unavoidable.

With his playoff triumph at the Las Vegas Invitational, Woods became a PGA Tour winner quicker and younger than Nicklaus, who claimed his first tour win with a splash -- at the 1962 U.S. Open, in his 18th tournament as a professional.
Nicklaus was 22 years, four months when he won for the first time on tour, while Woods was 20 years, nine months.

Woods is not the youngest to have won on tour. He does not even rate in the top 10. The legendary Gene Sarazen won three times as a 20 year old in 1922. But Woods is the second youngest in the last three decades.

Since Raymond Floyd won the 1963 St Petersburg Open at the age of 20 years, six months, the only other player to win at a younger age than Woods has been Phil Mickelson, the leading money winner on the tour this season with $1,620,999.
The left-handed Mickelson was 20 years, six months when he won the 1991 Tucson Open as an amateur.

While it is interesting to compare Woods with Nicklaus, since Tiger is widely regarded as the greatest prospect since the Golden Bear, Mickelson may offer a better comparison because he is of the same generation.
Mickelson, the 1990 U.S. amateur champion, did not turn pro until June 1992, some 17 months after his Tucson victory.
He did not win on tour in 1992, but won twice in 1993, once in 1994, once in 1995 and has triumphed four times this year.
Mickelson, 26, has accumulated nine tour victories at a younger age than anyone since Nicklaus, who had posted an incredible 17 wins before his 26th birthday.
As for the major championships, Mickelson has challenged several times without winning. His best results were a third at this year's Masters, and third at the '94 PGA Championship.
Mickelson did not contend in a major during his amateur days, and neither did Woods, who satisfied another significant objective with his maiden win in Las Vegas.
Woods, who relinquished his automatic spot in the Masters as Amateur champion when he turned pro, booked his berth in the 1997 field by claiming a tournament title.
Now he can start chasing the first of what Nicklaus predicts could be a double-digit collection of Green Jackets.
